Jinx
JINKS
noun / interjection / verb (Gen X slang)
From jynx, the wryneck, a bird the ancient Greeks bound to a wheel in love-charms (Greek iynx), hence a charm or spell. Jinx for a person or thing that brings bad luck is American slang by about 1910, common in baseball writing. For Gen X children it was also a schoolyard game: when two people say the same word at the same moment, the first to shout "Jinx!" silences the other until his name is spoken — or, by the common rule, until he is bought a Coke.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jinx has two lives in Gen X memory. On the playground it was a game: two kids say the same thing at the same time, one yells "Jinx! You owe me a Coke!" and the other must stay silent until someone speaks his name. At the ballgame and on the school bus it was a superstition: don’t mention the no-hitter, you’ll jinx it; don’t say we’ll win, you’ll jinx us. The game is harmless fun. The superstition is worth a closer look, because the word comes from the jynx, a bird the Greeks used in spells. To fear a jinx is to believe that words or luck can bend events apart from God. Scripture answers that fear with a Sovereign. "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD" (Pro 16:33). Balaam, hired to curse Israel, discovered that "there is no enchantment against Jacob, neither is there any divination against Israel" (Num 23:23). The Lord "frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad" (Isa 44:25), and He tells His people, "Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven" (Jer 10:2). Not one sparrow falls "without your Father" (Mat 10:29). A father can play jinx at the dinner table and laugh about the Coke; then, when the team is up in the ninth and someone whispers "don’t jinx it," he can smile and say: nobody can jinx what God has ordained. Speak freely; the Lord holds the game.

Webster 1828 Definition

From the jynx, a bird used in Greek charms, through American baseball slang (c. 1910) for a bringer of bad luck, to the schoolyard game of simultaneous speech; Scripture answers the superstition: the whole disposing of the lot is of the LORD (Pro 16:33).

expand to see more

JINX, n., interj., and v. (Gen X schoolyard slang; American from c. 1910) A person, thing, or word thought to bring bad luck; as an interjection, the call in the game of simultaneous speech. "Jinx! You owe me a Coke!" "Don’t say it — you’ll jinx it."

The game: whoever calls "Jinx!" first silences the other until his name is spoken; local rules vary on how the silence is lifted.

Superstition sense: to jinx a winning streak by speaking of it; jinxed, dogged by bad luck; a fixture of sports and theater lore.

No entry in Webster 1828 for jinx or its likely source jynx (the wryneck bird of Greek charm-magic); the word entered American slang in the early 20th century.

Decode for parents: play the game, but teach that no word or omen can jinx what God has ordained.

Key Scripture

Pro 16:33 — "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD."

Num 23:23 — "Surely there is no enchantment against Jacob, neither is there any divination against Israel: according to this time it shall be said of Jacob and of Israel, What hath God wrought!"

Isa 44:25 — "That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad; that turneth wise men backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish;"

Jer 10:2 — "Thus saith the LORD, Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them."

Mat 10:29 — "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father."

Modern Corruption

Jinx keeps alive, in a child’s game and a fan’s fear, the old belief that words and omens can bend events; Scripture answers with a God who disposes every lot and against whose people there is no enchantment.

expand to see more

The superstition under the game. The playground jinx is a test of quick reflexes and nothing more. The ballpark jinx is something else: the quiet belief that saying a thing aloud can spoil it, that luck is a force with a will of its own. That belief is a small piece of paganism wearing a ball cap. Its root is literal — the Greek wryneck bound to a wheel in love-spells — and its logic is the logic of the heathen who are "dismayed at the signs of heaven" (Jer 10:2). The Christian has no reason to be dismayed.

No enchantment against Jacob. Balaam was paid to speak a curse over Israel and could not make it stick: "there is no enchantment against Jacob" (Num 23:23). The lot falls into the lap, but the LORD disposes it (Pro 16:33); He frustrates the tokens of liars (Isa 44:25); not a sparrow falls without the Father (Mat 10:29). A child who knows this can say "we’re going to win" and lose without fear, because nothing he said changed anything God decreed. Providence is the end of superstition.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek iynx (the wryneck, a charm-bird) → Latin and English jynx → American jinx (c. 1910, baseball) → the schoolyard game; Scripture: the disposing of the lot is of the LORD (Pro 16:33).
